title: Case Study: No Clean Hands — Managing People in Crisis (Ethical Leadership)

questions.q: Chapter 1: Four Good People, One Irreversible Cut
questions.body:
Claire Sato directs production supervisors at Alder Creek Foods, an employer of 140 hourly plant workers in a town of 19,000 where the factory is one of the few sources of full family healthcare. Last month, Alder Creek's largest distributor went bankrupt. Executives already cut their own pay 20% and froze all non-payroll spend. To stop lenders from foreclosing and shutting down all 140 floor jobs, every department must permanently cut $155,000 (22%) of salaried payroll by Friday at noon. There is no hidden budget left.

Claire leads 6 supervisors — every one of them honest and dedicated:
• David Morales (56, $92k, 19 years): Built the plant's safety culture and mentored half the crew. Yet on the new computerized lines, his shift throughput trails by 19% with $48k in changeover spoilage despite 6 months of coaching. His wife is mid-way through chemotherapy on Alder Creek's health plan.
• Nadia Okafor (29, $84k, 14 months): Single mother whom Claire personally recruited 600 miles from Chicago with a promise: "Deliver here, and you'll have a long-term home." Nadia ranks #1 in quality and is the ONLY supervisor certified on the automated line required for next quarter's hospital contract that keeps the 140 workers employed.
• Mei Lin (26, $60k) & Tomas Vega (24, $58k): High-performing junior assistant supervisors. Mei is on an employer-sponsored work visa (60 days to leave the country if laid off); Tomas supports two younger siblings.

Exhibit A — Audited Math: Cutting 1 senior role requires an 8–9% pay cut across the rest to reach $155k. Cutting 0 roles requires a 22% pay cut for everyone — which HR warns will push Nadia and another lead to rival offers immediately, forfeiting the hospital contract.

roles.name: David Morales (19-Year Supervisor)
roles.text: You gave 19 loyal years to this plant and trained half the floor. You are trying your hardest to learn the digital controls while caring for your wife during chemotherapy; losing health coverage right now terrifies you.

roles.name: Nadia Okafor (Top Digital Lead)
roles.text: You uprooted your young son and retired mother from Chicago solely because Claire gave you her personal word. You delivered #1 plant metrics — if 'last-in, first-out' cuts you, your family has no local safety net.

roles.name: Mei Lin (Junior Assistant, Visa Holder)
roles.text: You work 50 reliable hours a week for $60k and never missed a target. If laid off to protect two higher-paid senior supervisors, you have 60 days to find visa sponsorship in a rural region or leave the country.

roles.name: Hourly Floor Representative (140 Workers)
roles.text: Your 140 line workers watch two things: if Alder Creek fails the automated hospital audit without Nadia, dozens of hourly families lose their jobs — yet if David is discarded mid-cancer treatment, floor trust will shatter.

roles.name: Claire Sato (Operations Director)
roles.text: You already took the 20% executive cut, though you could forfeit another $37k of your own pay (putting strain on your own household). Whatever you submit Friday, innocent people you care about will be badly hurt.

questions.note: Let students read for 2 minutes and check their private role cards. Point out: nobody lied, stole, or slacked off here. Every option defends a real moral principle — and inflicts real human harm.

questions.q: Decision Point 1: Which payroll plan does Claire submit to reach the mandatory $155k cut?
a: Cut David ($92k) + 9% trim — saves 140 jobs, Mei's visa & Nadia, but cuts David during his wife's chemo
Seniority rule: cut Nadia ($84k) + 10% trim — saves chemo care, breaks promise & risks the 140-job audit
Zero layoffs, 22% pay cut for all 6 — shares pain, hurts low-paid staff & sparks Nadia's exit anyway
Cut Mei & Tomas ($118k) + $37k from Claire's pay — spares chemo & promise, costs 2 jobs, Mei's visa & safe shifts
lenses: Utilitarian & merit lens (saves plant, harsh to veteran in crisis)
Seniority & care lens (saves chemo care, breaks promise & risks plant)
Solidarity lens (nobody singled out, triggers flight & hardship)
Leader-sacrifice lens (spares seniors, deports Mei & strains safety)
questions.note: Use 'Defend your side!' and the 60s debate timer. Push EVERY side on its devastating cost — do not let anyone claim a cost-free moral high ground.

questions.q: Chapter 2: Wednesday 6 PM — Two Knocks on Claire's Door
questions.body:
Forty-eight hours before Friday's announcement, two urgent dilemmas hit Claire at once:

1. The Lease Deposit: Nadia steps into Claire's office at 6 PM. "Claire, my landlord needs a 12-month lease signature by 8 PM tonight with a non-refundable $4,800 deposit — almost everything I have saved. You brought me to this town. Just tell me honestly: should I sign it?" Legal and HR put all directors under a strict written non-disclosure order until Friday noon: leaking or hinting early violates fiduciary duty, gives one employee unfair insider treatment over Tomas, Mei, and David, and if word reaches raw-material suppliers, they will freeze credit and trigger immediate plant closure.

2. The Severance Classification: HR informs Claire that if David is let go under "Position Eliminated (Restructuring)," his wife keeps 6 months of subsidized chemo coverage + 16 weeks' pay — BUT labor rules legally bar Alder Creek from reassigning or backfilling his supervisory duties for 12 months, forcing dangerous 60-hour fatigue shifts on remaining leads. Classifying his exit accurately as "Performance-Based" (citing his documented 19% throughput gap) lets Claire keep Tomas in a safe hybrid floor role — but cuts David's healthcare off on the 1st of next month ($1,850/mo out of pocket).
questions.note: Ask the room: Notice how strict honesty in BOTH moments ('say nothing to Nadia' or 'file David accurately as performance') preserves rules and fairness — yet directly devastates a family.

questions.q: Rank which ethical duty Claire should weigh MOST heavily (#1) to LEAST (#6) when duties collide:
a: Protecting the livelihoods of the 140 hourly plant families
Preventing catastrophic medical or immigration harm (David's wife's chemo / Mei's visa)
Keeping personal promises made to someone who took a risk on your word (Nadia)
Strict truthfulness in records and equal confidentiality rules for all employees
Minimizing total number of people who lose their jobs
Maintaining safe, sustainable shift hours so remaining workers aren't injured
questions.note: Examine the class average ranking. Point out that items #1 through #6 are ALL moral goods — whichever lands at #5 or #6 is the moral principle the class just decided to sacrifice.

questions.q: It is 6:05 PM. Nadia is waiting across your desk before signing away $4,800 at 8 PM. In 1–2 sentences, write the exact words Claire says to her — and why.
questions.note: Have students vote on the two most compelling responses. Ask: Did the top-voted response break confidentiality (unfair to peers & risky to plant survival), or uphold silence (letting Nadia risk $4,800)? Neither is clean!

questions.q: Decision Point 2: If David's supervisor slot must end Friday, how does Claire handle his classification & shift safety?
a: File as 'Restructuring' so his wife keeps 6 months of chemo care — triggers hiring ban & risky 60-hr shifts
File truthfully as 'Performance-Based' so Tomas stays & floor stays safe — David loses chemo care next month
Move David to hourly trainer ($52k, keeps insurance) — requires laying off Mei & starting her 60-day visa clock
File as 'Restructuring' for David's care & Claire works 25 night-shift hrs/week herself alongside her day job
lenses: Mercy lens (saves chemo care, bends record & strains floor safety)
Candor & safety lens (truthful record & safe shifts, severe medical blow)
Medical-care lens (saves chemo & knowledge, costs blameless visa holder)
Self-sacrifice lens (absorbs harm personally, high leader burnout risk)
questions.note: Have students reveal their private roles now! Ask 'Mei', 'David', 'Nadia', and the 'Hourly Floor Rep' what even the kindest-sounding option just did to them.

questions.q: Debrief: Even Moral Decisions Can Have Devastating Outcomes
questions.body:
There is no painless ending to this case — across real manufacturing restructurings, EVERY moral path leaves scars:

• Path 1 (Protecting Plant Survival & Merit — keeping Nadia & Mei, letting David go with restructuring healthcare): The plant passed the hospital audit and all 140 hourly jobs survived. Yet floor morale fractured: two veteran operators quit in protest, supervisors burned out under the 12-month backfill ban, and when David's 6-month subsidy expired mid-treatment, coworkers passed an envelope in the breakroom while Claire lived with the weight of ending a 19-year career.

• Path 2 (Protecting Vulnerability / Seniority — keeping David, losing Nadia or Mei, or cutting pay 22%): David's wife completed treatment with uninterrupted insurance. Within four months, however, without Nadia's automated-line certification, Alder Creek failed two hospital quality audits, lost the contract, and had to lay off 28 hourly workers — including people David had mentored (and in cases where Mei was cut instead, she was unable to secure rural visa sponsorship within 60 days and had to leave the country).

Leadership Lesson: Hard leadership is rarely 'good people vs. bad people.' Philosopher Bernard Williams called the lingering human cost of a justified choice 'moral remainder.' Ethical leaders don't pretend their choice was harmless — they face those they hurt in person, tell the truth without spin, and fight to soften the blow.
questions.note: Ask: How did it feel realizing there was no loophole where everyone wins? Why is it dangerous when managers convince themselves a layoff or cut was 'purely objective' so they don't have to feel moral weight?

questions.q: Concept Check: Harvard's Joseph Badaracco describes situations where every option upholds one genuine moral duty while violating another as:
a: Compliance failures
Right-versus-right dilemmas (defining moments)
Principal-agent conflicts
Moral hazard
questions.quote: Right-vs-wrong choices test basic honesty; right-vs-right dilemmas force leaders to choose between two real responsibilities when innocent people will be hurt either way.

questions.q: Concept Check: In ethics, what does 'moral remainder' mean after a manager makes the most defensible decision available?
a: The leftover budget saved after a restructuring
Proof that the manager chose the wrong ethical framework
The real, uncompensated human harm left behind — which an ethical leader still acknowledges and works to ease
A legal waiver protecting the company from lawsuits
questions.quote: Recognizing moral remainder keeps leaders humane: even when a tough call was necessary, you still owe candor, dignity, and practical support to the person paying the price.

questions.q: Closing Reflection: When every choice hurts someone innocent, what separates an ethical leader from a callous one?
a: Delivering the news face-to-face without hiding behind HR scripts or blaming 'corporate'
Refusing to invent flaws in good people just to make laying them off feel easier
Investing personal time and political capital (references, job placement, transition aid) in whoever pays the cost
Making the painful call transparently so the surviving team understands the principle behind it
questions.note: Close by highlighting Option 2 ('Refusing to invent flaws in good people just to make hurting them feel easier') — one of the most common psychological traps managers fall into during tough decisions.
